data.title: Meduza: Why neither Russia nor Ukraine can turn the tide of the war — and how they still pull off successful offensives like Kyiv’s Operation Vivaldi
data.summary: Ukrainian soldiers who took part in Operation Vivaldi say a new tactic made their successful offensive near the Siverskyi Donets River north of Sloviansk possible. They are withholding the details so they can exploit the Russian army’s vulnerabilities again. Judging solely by the available evidence — videos published by both sides — the offensive’s pace and methods were no different from those of other operations in the full-scale war: Ukrainian forces spent months “chipping away” at the enemy’s defenses. They used similar methods in the Zaporizhzhia region this summer, as did Russian forces near Dobropillia over the summer and fall. Small assault groups advanced mainly by infiltration. There was not even a hint of maneuver warfare; the advance was 10–15 kilometers deep, typical for this stage of the war. What is preventing the two armies from breaking the positional stalemate? What does fighting look like today? How do soldiers counter drones on the front lines? And is there any reason to expect the dynamics of the war to change anytime soon?

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/11/12/.label: Meduza: Why neither Russia nor Ukraine can turn the tide of the war — and how they still pull off successful offensives like Kyiv’s Operation Vivaldi

This leads to flight cancellations and delays — as a rule, neither passengers nor airport staff can predict how long they will last. People caught in this situation before a flight are left alone with their problems: their plans are disrupted, staff give no clear instructions, and airlines try to save money on compensation. At the same time, the airports themselves were not designed to handle passengers from dozens of flights getting stranded simultaneously.
